content: A pressure ulcer is defined as a localized area of damage to the skin and/or underlying tissue, typically occurring over a bony prominence, caused by pressure or a combination of pressure and shear forces. Phototherapy, which involves the use of light or laser as a non-surgical, adjunctive treatment to promote healing, has gained attention in recent years. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of phototherapy on the healing of pressure ulcers. A comprehensive search was conducted in January 2014 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Wounds Group Specialised Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, and EBSCO CINAHL. The search was not restricted by language or publication date. The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared phototherapy (in addition to standard care) with sham phototherapy, another type of phototherapy, or standard care alone. Two reviewers independently assessed the relevance and design of the studies, extracted data, and evaluated the quality of the included trials. Efforts were made to contact study authors to obtain missing data. Disagreements were resolved through consensus and consultation with a third reviewer. Seven RCTs involving a total of 403 participants were identified. All trials were assessed as having an unclear risk of bias. Six trials compared phototherapy with standard care, while one trial compared phototherapy with sham phototherapy. Only one trial included a third group that received a different type of phototherapy. Overall, the evidence was insufficient to determine the effectiveness of phototherapy in healing pressure ulcers. Three studies reported on the time to complete healing. Two of these studies found that the group treated with ultraviolet (UV) light had a shorter mean time to complete healing compared to the control group, with a mean difference of -2.13 weeks (95% confidence interval [CI]: -3.53 to -0.72, P = 0.003). However, another study reported that the laser-treated group had a longer mean time to complete healing compared to the control group, with a mean difference of 5.77 weeks (95% CI: -0.25 to 11.79). These findings should be interpreted cautiously due to the small sample sizes and the possibility that the results occurred by chance. Three studies reported the proportion of ulcers that healed, but the results were inconsistent. One study used a different outcome measure, and the other two studies had varying treatment durations, making it impossible to combine the data and draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness of phototherapy. Adverse effects were reported in only two studies. One study reported a risk ratio (RR) of 0.72 (95% CI: 0.18 to 2.80) for adverse events, while another study reported an RR of 0.89 (95% CI: 0.71 to 1.12). These estimates were imprecise, and the data were based on the number of events rather than the number of individuals experiencing events. Five studies reported on the rate of change in ulcer area, but three of these studies found no statistically significant difference between the phototherapy and control groups. Due to differences in the outcome measures used, pooling of data was not performed. The trials included in this review were of low quality, with unclear methods for randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding of outcome assessors. None of the studies reported on important outcomes such as quality of life, length of hospital stay, pain, or cost. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the effects of phototherapy on pressure ulcer healing is highly uncertain. The quality of the evidence is very low due to the unclear risk of bias and the small number of trials available. It is not possible to determine whether phototherapy provides benefit or causes harm in this context. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify the potential role of phototherapy in the treatment of pressure ulcers.
